plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.8.4
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the derivation of the integral formula for fluid force on a submerged vertical surface. Panel (a): a cross-section of a fluid environment showing a blob-shaped surface submerged vertically, with the depth axis pointing downward; depth bounds a and b are marked with dashed red lines, depth h(x) is labeled from the fluid surface to the current level x, and width w(x) is shown as a horizontal segment across the surface at depth x. Panel (b): the same surface divided into n horizontal strips A1, A2, ..., An by partition points a = x0, x1, ..., x_{n-1}, b = xn along the depth axis. Panel (c): a close-up of the kth strip showing the sampling point x*_k between x_{k-1} and xk, with the strip approximated as a rectangle of width w(x*_k) and height Delta_xk, and depth h(x*_k) labeled. The figure sets up the Riemann sum F approx sum rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta_xk whose limit yields the fluid force integral F = integral from a to b of rho h(x) w(x) dx.

interactionPlan.concept: The fluid force on a submerged vertical surface is found by slicing the surface into thin horizontal strips, approximating each strip's force as pressure times area (rho * h(x*_k) * w(x*_k) * Delta_x_k), and taking the limit of the Riemann sum as the strips become infinitely thin, yielding F = integral from a to b of rho h(x) w(x) dx.
elements: fluid environment: light-blue filled rectangle representing the fluid, with a wavy horizontal line at the top marking the free surface
vertical depth axis on the left with arrowhead pointing downward (depth increases downward)
irregular blob-shaped vertical surface (tan/beige fill, black outline) submerged in the fluid — the same shape in all three panels
panel (a): dashed red horizontal lines at depths a and b from the axis to the surface

panel (a): depth labels a, x, b on the axis; double-headed arrow labeled h(x) from the fluid surface down to depth x; horizontal segment labeled w(x) spanning the blob's width at depth x with black endpoint dots

panel (b): partition of the depth axis a = x0, x1, x2, x3, ..., x_{n-1}, b = xn with dashed red lines and horizontal strip dividers across the blob, strips labeled A1, A2, A3, ..., An with vertical ellipsis dots

panel (c): magnified kth strip shown as a green rectangle spanning the blob, with depth labels x_{k-1}, x*_k (sampling point, red dashed line through it), x_k; double-headed arrow labeled Delta_x_k for strip height; double-headed arrow labeled h(x*_k) from the surface to the strip; horizontal double arrow labeled w(x*_k) beneath the strip for its width
panel labels (a), (b), (c)
readout area showing the running approximation F ≈ sum of rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta_x_k and the exact integral value

interactions.label: Strip index k
interactions.teaches: Each strip contributes one term rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta_x_k: deeper strips have larger pressure h(x*_k), while the strip's width w(x*_k) follows the blob's shape — sweeping k shows both factors changing from strip to strip

interactions.label: Number of strips n
interactions.teaches: Refining the partition makes each rectangular strip a better approximation of the surface, so the Riemann sum converges to the exact fluid force integral — the sum is the approximation, the limit is the integral

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Collapsing panels (a)-(c) into one view connects the whole construction: partition the depth axis, pick a sampling depth in each strip, and accumulate the strip forces into the total

demo_steps.title: One strip, one term
demo_steps.narration: With n = 6 strips, the highlighted strip A_k is approximated by a rectangle of width w(x*_k) and height Delta_x_k at depth h(x*_k). Drag k to see how depth and width — and therefore the strip's force contribution — vary down the surface.

demo_steps.title: Deeper means more pressure
demo_steps.narration: Move k toward the bottom: h(x*_k) grows steadily while w(x*_k) widens and narrows with the blob's outline, so the force per strip is a product of two competing effects.

demo_steps.title: Refine the partition
demo_steps.narration: Increase n: the strips get thinner, the green rectangular approximation hugs the blob more closely, and the running sum visibly converges to the exact integral F = integral_a^b rho h(x) w(x) dx.

demo_steps.title: The whole construction at once
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the animated single panel to watch the partition form, each strip light up in sequence, and its force term accumulate into the total — the Riemann sum built step by step.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Fluid force is not pressure times total area at one depth — pressure varies with depth, so the surface must be sliced into strips whose individual forces rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta_x_k are summed, and the limit of that sum is the integral F = integral_a^b rho h(x) w(x) dx.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the same irregular tan blob (rounded top, bulging upper-right, a concave inward notch on its lower-right, tapering to a rounded bottom-left) submerged in a light-blue fluid with a wavy free-surface line at the top of every panel. Depth axis on the left pointing downward — emphasize that depth increases downward, unlike typical graphs. Use dashed red for depth reference lines (a, b, partition levels, x*_k), black dots for endpoints of width segments, and italic serif math labels (h(x), w(x), A1...An, x*_k, Delta_x_k). The kth-strip highlight should fill the strip green as in panel (c), with a simultaneous callout showing its h(x*_k) arrow from the surface, w(x*_k) width arrow, and Delta_x_k height. Include a live numeric readout comparing the Riemann sum at the current n against the exact integral value so convergence in the refinement step is visible numerically as well as visually. In the animated single-panel view, sequentially highlight strips from A1 downward, adding each term to a displayed running sum.

authoredContext:
Suppose that a flat surface is immersed vertically in a fluid of weight density ρ and that the submerged portion of the surface extends from x = a to x = b along an x-axis whose positive direction is down (Figure 5.8.4a). For a ≤ x ≤ b, suppose that w(x) is the width of the surface and that h(x) is the depth of the point x. Define what is meant by the fluid force F on the surface, and find a formula for computing it. The basic idea for solving this problem is to divide the surface into horizontal strips whose areas may be approximated by areas of rectangles. These area approximations, along with inequalities (4), will allow us to create a Riemann sum that approximates the total force on the surface. By taking a limit of Riemann sums we will then obtain an integral for F. To implement this idea, we divide the interval [a, b] into n subintervals by inserting the points x1, x2,...,xn−1 between a = x0 and b = xn. This has the effect of dividing the surface into n strips of area Ak,k = 1, 2,...,n (Figure 5.8.4b). It follows from (4) that the force Fk on the kth strip satisfies the inequalities ρh(xk−1)Ak ≤ Fk ≤ ρh(xk)Ak or, equivalently, h(xk−1) ≤ Fk ρAk ≤ h(xk) Since the depth function h(x) increases linearly, there must exist a point x∗ k between xk−1 and xk such that h(x∗ k ) = Fk ρAk or, equivalently, Fk = ρh(x∗ k )Ak We now approximate the area Ak of the kth strip of the surface by the area of a rectangle of width w(x∗ k ) and height _x000b_xk = xk − xk−1 (Figure 5.8.4c). It follows that Fk may be approximated as Fk = ρh(x∗ k )Ak ≈ ρh(x∗ k ) · w(x∗ k )_x000b_xk Adding these approximations yields the following Riemann sum that approximates the total
